1091.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
1091.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak turns the usual order around: the pain that makes the soul long for God is its cure, while comfort that makes it forget Him is the real sickness.
1091.tie_back: The Kural's beloved has one look that wounds and another that heals; Guru Nanak likewise sees the ache of longing and its cure as bound together, with the pain itself leading to the remedy.
1091.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1091._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it shares the paradox of a pain that is also a cure, but Guru Nanak is speaking of spiritual longing for God, not a lover's glance, and the two looks of the Kural have no direct equivalent.

1092.quote_or_event: “He is so beautiful to my eyes; beholding Him, I have been bewitched.”
1092.explanation: In Raag Asa, Guru Arjan speaks as the bride-soul who has only to see her Lord to be completely captivated.
1092.tie_back: The Kural says even a stolen glance is more than half of love's joy; Guru Arjan likewise makes a single sight of the Beloved enough to captivate the soul.
1092.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 397, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1092._accuracy_note: Partial match: both stress the power of a single look, but the Kural's point is the furtive glance from the beloved, while Gurbani's longing is spiritual (the soul seeing God), not romantic.

1093.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field.”
1093.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak describes the spiritual life as a farm, with saram (modesty, or by another reading, effort) as the water that makes the crop of Naam grow.
1093.tie_back: In the Kural the girl's modest bowing of the head is water poured on the young plant of love; Guru Nanak too names modesty as the water that makes a crop grow.
1093.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1093._accuracy_note: Striking shared image of modesty as water on a growing crop, but Guru Nanak's crop is the Name of God, not human love, and some Punjabi commentators read saram as effort rather than modesty.

1094.quote_or_event: “He watches over all, but none see Him. How wonderful this is!”
1094.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak marvels that God looks on every creature while remaining unseen by them.
1094.tie_back: In the Kural the girl looks at the lover only when he is not looking; Guru Nanak's wonder is a Lord who always looks on us while we fail to see Him.
1094.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 30), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1094._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the pattern of seeing without being seen is shared, but Japji is about God and creation, with no shyness or courtship involved.

1095.quote_or_event: “The Truth does not remain hidden, even though one may try to hide it.”
1095.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Amar Das says that the divine light within a person shows itself even when he tries to keep it concealed.
1095.tie_back: The girl in the Kural will not look straight at her lover, yet her sidelong smile gives her away; Guru Amar Das says what is truly within cannot stay hidden.
1095.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 232, Raag Gauri, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1095._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the idea that what is inside cannot be hidden fits, but the Guru means the Truth of God in a devotee, not a girl's concealed love.

1096.quote_or_event: “Without being spoken, without being told, You know all, O Searcher of hearts.”
1096.explanation: In Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan says God, the Antarjami or knower of hearts, understands what is within a person without any words being needed.
1096.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the beloved speaks like a stranger, the true feeling behind the words is quickly understood; Guru Arjan's Lord reads the heart directly, whatever the words.
1096.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1228, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1096._accuracy_note: Partial match: both say the inner meaning is known apart from the words, but in Gurbani it is God who knows the heart, not one lover reading another.

1097.quote_or_event: “his father teaches him, and scolds him so many times, but still, he hugs him close in his embrace.”
1097.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan compares God to a father whose child keeps making mistakes: he scolds the child many times, yet his scolding hides no anger, and he takes the child back into his arms.
1097.tie_back: The Kural reads sharp words that hold no anger as a sign of hidden love; Guru Arjan's father likewise speaks harshly while his heart stays loving.
1097.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 624, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1097._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: harsh words that hide love are the common point, but Gurbani's image is a father and child (God and the devotee), not lovers acting like strangers.

1098.quote_or_event: “Renouncing selfishness and conceit, I seek His Sanctuary, and speak sweet words to Him.”
1098.explanation: In Barah Maha in Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan describes the soul-bride humbly pleading with her Husband Lord in the hope that He will turn to her with kindness.
1098.tie_back: In the Kural the lover looks at the girl imploringly and she softens and smiles; Guru Arjan's bride also pleads humbly and hopes the Beloved will soften toward her.
1098.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1098._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the humble pleading lover is shared, but the Gurbani verse is the soul's spiritual prayer to God and does not describe the beloved's answering smile.

1099.quote_or_event: “Only those who taste it know its sweet taste, like the mute, who eats the candy, and only smiles.”
1099.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak says the sweetness of the Lord's Name is known only to those who have tasted it, and they cannot explain it to anyone else.
1099.tie_back: The Kural says the cool look that lovers give each other in public is understood only by lovers; Guru Nanak too says only those who have known the love can read it.
1099.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 635, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1099._accuracy_note: Partial match on the idea of a private experience that only insiders understand; Gurbani speaks of the spiritual taste of Naam, not of lovers' looks, and its love is spiritual rather than romantic.

1100.quote_or_event: “Says Nanak, the Saints savor this sublime essence, like the mute, who tastes the sweet candy, but only smiles.”
1100.explanation: In Raag Kaanra, Guru Arjan compares the joy of union with God to a mute person tasting sweets: the delight is complete, but it can only be shown by a smile, never put into words.
1100.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying that when two pairs of eyes agree, words are of no use; Guru Arjan likewise says the deepest joy of love is beyond speech.
1100.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1302, Raag Kaanra, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1100._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on love being beyond words; the Gurbani image is of the soul's union with God (spiritual, not romantic) and the medium is a smile rather than meeting eyes.
